3. Their hands are on the near, camera-side tops of the barrels in a forward-pushing posture. They are on the open-road side of the barrels, between the camera and the barrels.
4. The barrels lie on their sides with their round wooden ends facing left toward the left edge of the frame. A barrel on its side rolls perpendicular to those round ends, so these barrels move toward the sidewalk and wall or back toward the camera, not left-right along the road. The men are therefore pushing across the road toward the sidewalk, facing away from the camera.
5. The background side is blocked. Directly in front of the men, in the direction they face, is the raised sidewalk, the continuous white wall, and the white building. There is no gate or opening visible for them to have come through. They cannot have walked into their present positions from the top or background of the frame through that solid wall and building.
6. The foreground side is open. Directly behind the men, in the direction their backs face, is the open asphalt road with painted markings. That is the only unobstructed approach to the backs of the barrels.
7. The simplest path without an extra 90-degree turn is therefore a straight path from the bottom edge toward the top: entering from the bottom, bottom-center to bottom-right, and walking forward away from the camera to stand behind the barrels.
8. They more likely did not enter from the left edge walking rightward, and did not enter from the right edge walking leftward. Such a side entry would mean walking across the frame and then turning about 90 degrees to face the wall and get behind the barrels, which is an extra turn with no evidence for it. Their final facing directly away from the camera favors entry along the viewing axis from behind the camera.
